finding.headline: This household has no children, pets, or college costs, so family costs are zero.
details: Family costs total $0, and there are no college or big one-time costs to plan for.
Once retired, the basic yearly costs are about $28,000, or $2,333 a month. Housing is $11,160, food $4,071, transport $6,069, and health $6,720.
Health costs before Medicare at age 65 would be about $10,000 a year, and a nursing home stay could run $129,575 a year for about 3 years.

finding.headline: In retirement you would pay about 10% of withdrawals in tax, and no tax while working.
details: Working, you have no pay, so no income tax applies. In retirement, the plan takes about $24,338 a year from savings, and tax is about $3,018 a year, or 10% of that.
Draw on taxable savings and cash first, then 401(k) or pre-tax accounts, and Roth accounts last. Most of your savings, 76%, sit in pre-tax accounts, so those will carry most of the tax.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Check the order with a tax professional before you withdraw.

finding.headline: Your spending goal lasts in 95 of 100 market scenarios, using a simple plan.
details: The most you can spend each year and still be safe in 90 of 100 scenarios is $53,200, just above your $52,000 goal. The kept plan is a simple plan: stocks at 110 minus your age, so about 31% in stocks.
Your basic costs were paid in all 100 scenarios, and the goal ran out in 5 of 100. Markets are uncertain, so these results are not promises.

finding.headline: You can count on $53,200 a year: $28,000 for basics and $25,200 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $28,000 a year.
Your goal is $52,000 a year, which lasts in 95 of 100 scenarios, so the goal works; little is left for wishes beyond it, since $53,200 is only just above $52,000.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
You already get Social Security (from 70): the plan uses the $30,000 a year you gave.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 93. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.

worth_checking.title: An income annuity
worth_checking.why: You are one person with savings that may not last in a long life. An income annuity trades part of your savings for a fixed sum each year for life. The sum loses value to inflation and the money cannot be taken back. This is information only. This is something to look into, not a recommendation. I have not priced it.
